scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #7058: HELP! My computer can't talk to the laptops any more --
the laptop machine might as well be on another planet. The desktop people and
the laptop people sit on two different networks, and something between the two
halves must be wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone look at whatever
joins the two groups so I can reach the laptops again!!! Thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 routes between VLAN 10 (eth0.10,
  172.16.10.1) and VLAN 20 (eth0.20, 172.16.20.1) on its router-on-a-stick
  sub-interfaces, and mswitch1 trunks both VLANs. PC4 (172.16.10.x) reaches
  Laptop0 (172.16.20.x) with 0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of a sub-interface / trunk fault that is not
  present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- VLAN 10 cannot reach
VLAN 20 within Location A -- is NOT reproducible: router0's eth0.10 (172.16.10.1)
and eth0.20 (172.16.20.1) sub-interfaces are up with correct dot1Q tags, mswitch1
trunks both VLANs, and PC4 (VLAN 10) reaches Laptop0 (VLAN 20) with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: inter-VLAN routing is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the VLAN10->VLAN20
path, finds it working, checks router0's sub-interfaces and mswitch1's trunk, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a sub-interface misconfig or a trunk drop
to satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes router0's eth0.10/eth0.20 sub-interfaces are up and mswitch1 trunks both VLANs at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text: Router6 has a misconfigured iptables firewall on its FORWARD chain that drops all forwarded traffic originating from its WAN-side interface (eth2, connecting to router3). The chain contains four rules: a narrow ACCEPT for TCP port 80 from 172.16.10.0/24 to 172.18.51.1, followed by catch-all DROP rules for TCP, UDP, and all other protocols (including ICMP) — all scoped to inbound traffic on eth2. Since every packet from the desktop network (172.16.10.0/24, 172.16.20.0/24) arrives at router6 via eth2 after transiting router0→router1→router2→router3, these DROP rules silently discard ICMP, UDP, and TCP before the packets can be forwarded to the laptop network (172.18.50.0/24 on switch11 via mswitch2). This is why router6 can ping laptop4 directly (that traffic uses the OUTPUT chain, bypassing FORWARD entirely) while pc4 and all other devices upstream of router3 cannot reach laptop4 or laptop5 at all. The hit counters confirm it: rule 3 (DROP UDP) shows 26 packets matching — the traceroute UDP probes — and rule 4 (DROP all/ICMP) shows 13 packets matching — the ICMP echo requests from the ping tests. Root cause: router6's FORWARD chain has blanket DROP rules for all protocols entering on eth2, blocking the entire desktop-to-laptop traffic path. Corrective fix: remove the three DROP rules (`iptables -D FORWARD -i eth2 -p tcp -j DROP`, `-p udp`, and `-p 0`) and replace them with policy-aligned ACCEPT rules, or at minimum insert `iptables -I FORWARD 1 -p icmp -j ACCEPT` and appropriate stateful rules (`-m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED`) to restore bidirectional connectivity.
